title: Primary glioblastoma multiform (GBM) of the optic nerve and chiasma: A case report and systematic review of the literature
case_prompt:
A 77-year-old woman with no prior medical or familial history presented with progressive bilateral visual loss of more than eight weeks’ duration. The left eye became affected first, two months before presentation, followed by involvement of the right eye four weeks later. She had been evaluated at three outpatient clinics without diagnostic imaging. Two weeks before referral, she attended an emergency department because of worsening visual field disturbances.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a suspected lesion at the left optic chiasma. Subsequent brain MRI showed a space-occupying lesion in the left chiasma: it was isointense on T1 without contrast, relatively hyperintense on T2, and demonstrated contrast enhancement on T1 sequences.

Based on these findings, the lesion was initially presumed inflammatory and treated with dexamethasone. Despite corticosteroid therapy, her visual acuity continued to deteriorate. On ophthalmologic examination at our center, visual acuity was 12/20 in the right eye and only light perception in the left eye. Formal perimetry demonstrated a right quadrantanopia and severely restricted responses in the left eye. Laboratory tests for systemic inflammatory diseases, including sarcoidosis and toxoplasmosis, were negative. Given the rapid progression, lack of steroid response, and imaging consistent with a mass lesion, an open surgical biopsy was proposed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of an inflammatory optic neuropathy — “Initially, the lesion was believed to be an inflammatory process and treated with dexamethasone alone.”  
2. Exclusion of sarcoidosis or toxoplasmosis — “negative laboratory results for systemic inflammatory diseases (such as sarcoidosis or toxoplasmosis).”  
3. Suspicion of a neoplastic mass — “radiological differential diagnosis of a mass lesion … we proposed an open surgical biopsy.”
